Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer effectively uses exposition and summary in the first half of the story to establish the setting, historical context, and the congregation's sense of suburban security (such as summarizing the synagogue's migration from Detroit to Southfield, Rabbi Adler's background, and the brief backstory of the shooter). This background information is seamlessly woven into the real-time scenes of Barbara getting ready at home and attending the Sabbath service. When the climax occurs—the shooting on the *bima* and the subsequent panic—the narrative shifts almost entirely into vivid, real-time scene writing, using sensory details, action, and dialogue to heighten the tension and make the tragedy feel immediate and engaging.
